title: How Much Fruit Is on Your Coaching Tree?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that leaders should borrow the athletic idea of a coaching tree, the lineage of assistants a head coach has developed into head coaches themselves, as a measure of their own impact. The post explains how the tree works in sports, where a coach's standing rests on whether their knowledge transfers to others. It then moves the idea into ordinary organizations, claiming that the track record of people a leader has mentored is a clear mark of a special leader, whether those people thrive elsewhere or in the original organization. The suggested exercise is to chart the leaders you have developed and see where they are now. The author says this both reinforces the value of developing others and reminds a leader why the work matters. The piece closes by framing the tree as a picture of legacy and asking how much fruit one's own leadership is bearing.
points: A leader's legacy is best judged by the people they have developed, not only by their own results.
The athletic coaching tree works as a ready-made visual model of mentoring lineage that any organizational leader can adapt.
Mapping where your mentees now serve is offered as a motivating self-audit that reinforces the purpose of developing others.
Success of mentees counts whether it happens elsewhere or inside the original organization.
quotes: In the world of athletics, the coaches with a superlative Coaching Tree are considered the best of the best. Not only can they succeed with their own teams, but they can transfer their knowledge and skills to others.

If the head coach is an effective developer of talent, they push assistants to take the next level-job at another school or team. The best of these assistants become head coaches themselves and start the process all over with their own group of assistants.

Great leaders outside of athletics would be smart to consider their own Coaching Trees. A clear sign of a special leader is the track record of those they have mentored and developed, whether those mentees go on to great success elsewhere or inside the original organization.

Charting out the leaders you have developed and learning where they are now can be an illuminating exercise. Visualizing the impact you have had on others can reinforce the importance of developing others.

In college and professional athletics, Assistant Coaches serve in an apprentice role for Head Coaches. They develop their talents and skills under the tutelage and guidance of a successful coach as they learn the ropes about how to someday guide their own team.
Your Coaching Tree displays this legacy, so you know where you stand. How healthy is your tree?
